post_text:
I sat on my hands during that planning review until my knuckles went white.

A junior teammate was pitching a strategy I knew had a blind spot, and every instinct screamed at me to cut in.

The metrics were green. The system wasn’t.

Stepping in would have saved us four days of wasted effort. But taking the marker from his hand would have stripped his credibility in front of stakeholders, teaching him that my voice mattered more than his preparation.

I chose to stay quiet and let the room approve the path forward.

The friction hit us exactly where I anticipated the following week. Instead of swooping in with the fix, I asked him how he wanted to handle the recovery and cleared my calendar to back him up.

He owned the misstep, faced the stakeholders directly, and reworked the plan from the ground up.

His revised approach ended up simpler and more durable than the solution I had guarded in my own head.

We paid for that lesson with four days of lost progress, but we gained an engineer who no longer looks around the room for permission to lead.

Real leadership is absorbing the discomfort of watching someone stumble so they can build the muscle to stand.
lesson_extracted: Protecting a teammate's ownership is worth more than saving a few days of rework.
